title: Your Blended Margin Looks Healthy. Some of What You Sell Is Quietly Losing Money.
excerpt: A blended gross margin can hold steady for months while individual product or service lines move in opposite directions underneath it. Here's how that averaging hides real drift.
content:
The gross margin percentage on your monthly management report can hold steady for six months running while the business underneath it changes completely. Revenue grows, cost of goods grows roughly in step, and the number lands in a familiar, comfortable band every time you check it. Nothing about that steadiness tells you to look closer.

That is usually the least reliable signal in the report. A blended margin is an average, and averages exist to smooth movement, not reveal it. One product or service line can be losing margin every month while another compensates almost exactly, and the two shifts cancel out on the page long before either one gets noticed on its own.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is rarely a sudden margin collapse. It is the number quietly ceasing to mean what everyone assumes it means, while decisions keep getting made on the strength of a figure that no longer describes what is actually being sold.

The Number on the P&L Is an Average, Not a Verdict

A single gross margin percentage is a weighted blend of every product or service line, every customer segment, every job that moved through the business that month. When two lines shift in opposite directions by a similar amount, the blended figure barely moves, even though the underlying mix has changed materially. A line that used to carry forty percent of revenue might now carry sixty, and if that line runs a thinner margin than the rest, the blended number is being pulled down by volume even while headline revenue climbs.

This is exactly why margin can look stable through a period of real change. Growth is rarely spread evenly across everything a business sells. It concentrates in whatever is easiest to sell, easiest to deliver, or most in demand that quarter, and that is not always the most profitable part of the business.

Where the Averaging Usually Happens

The pattern shows up in a handful of familiar places. A service or product added to fill spare capacity during a quiet stretch, priced to win the work rather than to reflect its true cost, that never gets repriced once volume returns. A newer customer segment that needs more hand-holding or more customisation per dollar of revenue than the segment the business was originally built on. A discount that started as a one-off concession for a single client and quietly became the standing rate for an entire category of work. Input costs that rise on one line's materials while a service-based line's costs stay flat, so the blended movement looks smaller than it actually is on the line doing the damage.

None of these show up as a problem in the total. They show up as a blended margin that looks fine, sitting on top of two or three very different stories about what is actually making money.

What Splitting the Number by Line Actually Shows

Once margin gets broken down by product, service line or customer segment, the picture is rarely subtle. It is common to find one line running comfortably above the blended average and another running well below it, and for the low-margin line to be the one that has been getting the most sales attention and the most delivery hours over the past year. That is not a coincidence. Growth tends to flow toward whatever is easiest to say yes to, and the easiest yes is not always the most profitable one.

A structured line by line review of cost and margin is usually where this becomes visible for the first time, because it forces a keep, fix or scale decision on every revenue line individually, rather than leaving them to average each other out. Some lines genuinely deserve to be scaled. Some need a considered price review or a change in how they are delivered. A few are worth keeping exactly as they are, deliberately, once the owner can see what they are actually contributing.

Deciding What to Do With What You Find

The useful distinction is between a low-margin line that is there on purpose and one that is there by accident. A loss leader that fills capacity in a quiet month or opens the door to higher-margin work later can be a perfectly sound decision, as long as it is a decision and not a default. A line that has drifted to a low margin because nobody has repriced it since it started, or because its delivery cost has crept up unnoticed, is a different problem, and usually a fixable one.

The businesses that stay ahead of this are not doing anything exotic. They are simply looking at margin by line often enough that drift gets caught early, which is one of the reasons a fractional CFO partnership tends to include this as a standing item rather than a once-off exercise. Your bookkeeper's monthly reporting is doing exactly what it is designed to do, which is produce an accurate total. Reading what is inside that total is a separate piece of work.

Seeing the business this way rarely changes what you sell overnight. It changes where you put your attention next quarter, and which conversations with customers, suppliers or your own team are actually worth having first. If the blended number on your P&L has not moved much lately, that is worth a second look rather than a reason to relax. You can book a discovery call to walk through where your margin is actually coming from.

faqs.q: How do I work out the profit margin for each product or service I sell?
faqs.a: Start by allocating direct costs, materials, labour and any delivery-specific overhead to each product or service line rather than to the business as a whole, then calculate gross margin on each line separately. Most accounting software can support this with proper job or category tracking. A structured cost and margin review does this once in full and sets up the ongoing split so drift gets caught early next time.

faqs.q: Why does my overall gross margin stay steady even though costs keep rising?
faqs.a: A blended margin is an average across everything the business sells, so a cost increase on one line can be offset by growth or pricing strength on another, leaving the total looking unchanged. The movement is still happening underneath, it just is not visible until the numbers are split by line. That is usually the first sign worth investigating rather than dismissing.

faqs.q: What is a healthy gross margin percentage for an Australian SME?
faqs.a: There is no single healthy number, because it depends heavily on the industry, the cost structure and how much value-add sits in the product or service itself. What matters more than the industry benchmark is whether your own margin is trending in a known direction for a known reason, rather than being assumed to be fine because it has not moved much lately.

faqs.q: Should I stop selling a product or service line with low margin?
faqs.a: Not automatically. A low-margin line can be a deliberate loss leader, a capacity filler in a quiet period, or the entry point to higher-margin work later, and any of those can be a sound reason to keep it. The problem is a low-margin line that exists by accident, because nobody has repriced it or reviewed its delivery cost since it started.

faqs.q: What is the difference between gross margin and net profit margin?
faqs.a: Gross margin measures revenue less the direct cost of delivering a product or service, while net profit margin subtracts every other cost in the business, including overhead, wages not tied to delivery, and finance costs, to show what is actually left over. Both matter, but gross margin by line is usually where the earliest warning signs of a profitability problem show up.

faqs.q: What does a fractional CFO do differently from my bookkeeper or accountant?
faqs.a: Your bookkeeper or accountant is doing exactly what that role is designed to do, keeping the ledger accurate, the BAS lodged and the compliance obligations met. A fractional CFO sits on top of that accurate data and asks the commercial questions, including which parts of the business are genuinely profitable and what to do about the ones that are not.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help find which parts of my business are actually profitable?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO builds and maintains a margin-by-line view as a standing part of the monthly reporting rhythm, rather than as a one-off project, so drift between lines gets flagged while it is still small and easy to fix. That ongoing visibility is usually what separates a business that catches margin erosion early from one that discovers it at year end.
